messages.author: 7ab2d61d18fd7449
messages.subject: Matt trick reparametrization question
parts:
Dear all,

I have a quite complex model and I'm trying to improve the sampling
performance. I'm estimating it for psychophysical data which is already
hierarchical on the subject level but there is a group level as well. On
the group level I have tried to reparametrize it using what was referred
to in the FAQs as the Matt trick. I have now done it for several
parameters like this:

C_n[s] <- C_n_mean + e_C_n[s] * C_n_sigma;

Where e_C_n is drawn from normal(0,1) and C_n_mean (group mean)
contained in a certain range and C_n_sigma (group deviation) has a
half-Cauchy prior.

In some aspects it seems to work nicely, but there are also some
problems. Hence I have some questions regarding the e_C_n[s] terms:

* Do I understand it correctly that they can be considered error terms
on the lower level?
* Apparently I have to constrain the error terms. If I don't,
initialization fails. Is this normal?
* Are they allowed to become negative?
* C_n[s] is not supposed to be negative. However, if I give it a lower=0
or any other constraints, again initialization fails. Obviously this
happens when e_C_n[s] is drawn negative ... do I have to contain this
instead?
* Are their any other aspects / problems that can come up in the
posteriors of these error terms?

Many thanks in advance & best regards
Jan

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Matt trick reparametrization question
parts:
On Saturday, October 17, 2015 at 11:44:47 AM UTC-4, dqsIJan Tünnermann wrote:
C_n[s] <- C_n_mean + e_C_n[s] * C_n_sigma;

Where e_C_n is drawn from normal(0,1) and  C_n_mean (group mean)
contained in a certain range and  C_n_sigma (group deviation) has a
half-Cauchy prior.

In some aspects it seems to work nicely, but there are also some
problems. Hence I have some questions regarding the e_C_n[s] terms:

* Do I understand it correctly that they can be considered error terms
on the lower level?
If I were to refer to something as an error term, it would be e_C_n[s] * C_n_sigma. But you could just say group heterogeneity or something.

* Apparently I have to constrain the error terms. If I don't,
initialization fails. Is this normal?
* Are they allowed to become negative?
* C_n[s] is not supposed to be negative. However, if I give it a lower=0
or any other constraints, again initialization fails. Obviously this
happens when e_C_n[s] is drawn negative ... do I have to contain this
instead?

Matt tricking is traditionally for variables in the location-scale family, which does not include non-negative parameters. So, I think the normal distribution is not the right choice for C_n[s] if it is non-negative. You could use the geometric principles behind the Matt trick for a non-negative distribution by multiplying unit scale variables by a common value. In the simple case of an exponential distribution, it might be something like

parameters {
  real<lower=0> C_n_mean;
  vector<lower=0>[S] C_n_unit;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector<lower=0> C_n;
  C_n <- C_n_unit * C_n_mean;
}
model {
  C_n_unit ~ exponential(1);
  C_n_mean ~ something;
  ...
}

If that is too inflexible, you could do something similar with a gamma distribution instead of an exponential.

* Are their any other aspects / problems that can come up in the
posteriors of these error terms?

Possibly you have to tweak adapt_delta and / or max_treedepth.

Ben

thanks a lot for the hints.

[...]

Hmm. Actually, on the subject level I have four different types of parameters:

1) (those like C_n[s]) which are rate parameters of exponential functions (used on lower levels).
(some time ago I experimented with (inverse?)gamma priors for these in JAGS if I remember correctly, but dropped that for some reason.)

2) The second type of parameters is modeling a shift of the x-axis intercept of the psychometric function

3) The third type describes a plateau in the scale of the x-axis. Hence it is similar to type 2, but can only be positive.

4) The fourth type are weights or biases if you will.  They are neutral at 0.5 and range from 0 to 1 (the extremes are highly improbably, however).

Up to now I have been drawing the subject level versions all from normals, as described before for the C_n. 
Do the different types imply any better group level distributions? (I have the feeling that what you describe below may be good for the rate type parameters).

Many thanks and best regards
Jan

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Matt trick reparametrization question
parts:
On Saturday, October 17, 2015 at 1:45:52 PM UTC-4, dqsIJan Tünnermann wrote:
Up to now I have been drawing the subject level versions all from normals, as described before for the C_n. 
Do the different types imply any better group level distributions? (I have the feeling that what you describe below may be good for the rate type parameters).

I don't really know anything about this research area and what is the best distribution to use would depend on the data. The computational principles I was trying to emphasize are that --- among parameterizations that yield the same marginal posterior distributions for the parameters of interest --- you generally want the primitive parameters to all have unit scale and to be independent of each other a priori. That is what the Matt trick does for unrestricted variables from a location-scale family. That is not straightforward if the variable is restricted to be non-negative, because, at a minimum, you induce a lot of prior dependence between the location parameter and primitive parameters that are being scaled so that the resulting variable is non-negative. You could assume that the non-negative parameter is lognormal and do Matt trick stuff on the log scale. Or you can use a variety of non-negative distributions (like the exponential) that are closed under rescaling but do not have a location parameter. There are some other options but the other computation principle is that you want to avoid using the declared bounds on transformed parameters to reject proposals for the primitive parameters that imply a transformed parameter is negative.

Ben

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Matt trick reparametrization question
parts:
The utility of parameter expansion is usually limited to Gibbs samplers
and I’d be surprise if it proved useful here.  You really want to use
non-centered parameterizations (the more formal name of the “Matt trick”).

The trick is to decouple hierarchical parameters with a transformation.
For example, the standard parameterization

theta ~ normal(mu_pop, sigma_pop)

is bad because the group-level thetas are highly correlated with both
mu_pop and sigma_pop.  But if you do

theta_tilde ~ normal(0, 1)
theta = mu_pop + sigma_pop * theta_tilde

then theta_tilde becomes independent of mu_pop and sigma_pop,
yielding a nicer posterior.

You can do this for all kinds of distributions, but you’ll have to work
out the necessary transformations yourself.  For example, with an
exponential you could go from

theta ~ exponential(lambda_pop)

to

theta_tilde ~ exponential(1)
theta = lambda_pop * theta_tilde.

In practice I usually stick with generalized linear models, so leave
the thetas unconstrained and then constrain them using link functions,

theta_tilde ~ normal(0, 1)
theta = mu_pop + sigma_pop * theta_tilde
rho = exp(theta).

Dear Ben,

thanks again for the input. It really helps me to better understand what's going on. Probably the Matt trick thing is not suited for the group level parameters. I will try some sort of parameter expansion instead.

Best regards
Jan

thanks for suggestions! I ended up sticking with the non-centered parametrizations of normals where it had been working working before. For those parameters that sometimes flipped negative on the subject level (or did other weird things) I just kept the "bad" normal(mu,sig) draws. In a first test it worked okay (larger sampling currently running). So maybe those paras that behaved weirdly were already quite mobile and less likely of getting trapped. And reparametrization of critical ones may be sufficient ... let's see.

Best
Jan

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Matt trick reparametrization question
parts:
Non-centered parameterizations decouple the prior, but couple the likelihood.
The relative performance of centered vs non-centered parameterizations then
depends on how much data you have.  See, for example, http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906.
